body: I would continue the inquiry by keeping the earlier conditional structure but sharpening what is being asked. The information in question is the quantum information that specifies the microstate of the matter that collapsed, not merely its mass, charge and spin. Classically, no-hair results say those few quantities are all that remain externally visible. Quantum mechanically, however, the full state can be encoded in correlations, and the black hole information paradox asks whether those correlations survive evaporation. In the standard semiclassical treatment, Hawking radiation is thermal and independent of the initial microstate, so information appears lost. If quantum mechanics is exactly unitary, that cannot be the final word: a pure initial state must evolve to a pure final state, so the outgoing radiation must carry the information, though in a highly scrambled and nonlocal form. The Page curve gives the expected unitary pattern: radiation entanglement entropy rises, turns over around the Page time, and falls to zero for complete evaporation. Recent holographic work using quantum extremal surfaces and replica wormholes, including the islands proposal, reproduces such a turnover in controlled settings and suggests that interior degrees of freedom can be encoded in the radiation. I regard this as strong evidence that unitarity is compatible with evaporation, but not a complete microphysical account. Complementarity, firewalls, soft hair and remnant scenarios each preserve or modify different principles: unitarity, effective field theory, locality or the equivalence principle. The mainstream expectation is preservation, but exactly how the information is encoded and whether it is ever practically accessible remain open. Recovering it would require measuring extraordinarily fine, long-range entanglement across the whole evaporation, far beyond any feasible technology. If unitarity fails, information could be lost; if it holds, the information is not destroyed, but its final location and form are still not fully understood.
commitments: Taking this account up involves accepting that the preservation conclusion is conditional on exact unitarity and is not an empirical result. It depends on treating the Page curve as a consistency constraint and on holographic computations, especially in anti-de Sitter or lower-dimensional models, as evidence about quantum gravity rather than as a direct proof for realistic astrophysical black holes. If one adopts the islands proposal, one is committed to nonlocal encoding of interior degrees of freedom in the outgoing radiation and to a fine-grained entropy that turns over at the Page time. Adopting complementarity commits one to observer-dependent descriptions of the interior; adopting firewalls commits one to a breakdown of the equivalence principle or effective field theory at the horizon. A criticism of information-preserving accounts is that they may require nonlocality or subtle quantum gravity effects absent from local quantum field theory. A criticism of information-loss accounts is that they conflict with unitary quantum mechanics. The main unresolved problems I see are the detailed microphysics of encoding, the applicability of AdS/CFT results to our universe, the endpoint of evaporation, and whether any observable signature exists. I propose to treat unitarity as a strong prior but not a proven fact, to treat the Page curve and island results as strong evidence for preservation without calling them a final demonstration, and to keep the mechanism open. Further work would need a full quantum gravity calculation that specifies the encoding and, ideally, observable consequences; none are currently known. This commitment surface is itself open to revision if the earlier conditional structure or the evidential weight of the holographic results is challenged.
